appraisal_events.evidence: Cette liaison avec Mme de Forcheville... venait de faire perdre au duc de Guermantes, pour la deuxième fois, la possibilité de la présidence du Jockey et un siège de membre libre à l'Académie des Beaux-Arts... les deux frères... étaient arrivés à la déconsidération; meanwhile Odette 'se diminuait' catering to his whims, tending 'à redevenir... la dame en rose.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator reports that the duke's possessive late-life affair with Odette costs him prestigious institutional standing (paralleling Charlus's decline through Jupien), while Odette correspondingly abases herself back toward her earlier, lower social identity to keep him.

appraisal_events.evidence: Il n'était plus qu'une ruine, mais superbe... rongée comme une de ces belles têtes antiques trop abîmées mais dont nous sommes trop heureux d'orner un cabinet de travail... chose curieuse, lui qui jadis était presque ridicule... avait pris un aspect véritablement grand... la vieillesse l'avait fait encore plus qu'auguste, suppliant.
appraisal_events.explanation: Despite physical ruin, being mocked by Odette ('se moquait de lui'), and needing support to walk, the narrator explicitly and at length reframes the aged duke as newly grand and tragically dignified where he was once merely ridiculous; this admiring aestheticization dominates the paragraph even as frailty and humiliation persist alongside it.

status_effects.explanation: The affair explicitly costs him a second chance at the Jockey Club presidency and an Académie des Beaux-Arts seat, marking clear worldly déconsidération.
The narrator's extended, admiring portrait of his ruin as 'superbe' and 'véritablement grand' locally raises how he is regarded, even though this coexists with mockery and physical frailty.
Though long established as 'une femme du monde,' Odette is shown reducing herself to please the old duke, reverting toward her earlier identity as 'la dame en rose.'
The narrator states plainly that her life was rendered very unhappy by the duke's late-life affair with Odette.

ambiguities: The final paragraph's portrait of the duke is genuinely double-edged: the narrator's sustained aestheticizing admiration ('superbe', 'véritablement grand') coexists with Odette's mockery and his physical suppliant frailty, so E2 is read as mixed rather than purely positive or negative.
